Twenty-four comments

Good Beginner Piece.

I learned this number as a four part tune but I believe it to be a simple AB tune. I put this on my first recording project and I was ever so proud of it. Do you ever go back to those old recordings? They make your hair stand up on end and face twists in pain.

They say you are your own worst critic. I am sure you all could find something pretty awful to say about my playing back then. :)

I believe this piece is Irish. If I’m wrong - well - try it anyway.

↳ Posted by JACKB on June 7th, 2020.

Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’, X:6

An arrangement by Ellery Klein. A Shetland tune.

In terms of key, it sort of bridges a gap between A Aeolian and what we’d call A minor (raising the 7th a half step for a harmonic minor scale). A very interesting effect!

↳ Posted by greatawk on January 11th, 2021.

Re: Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’

The tune is in A dorian, the raised note is the 6th, not the 7th.

↳ Posted by jeff_lindqvist on January 11th, 2021.

Re: Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’

The seventh is also sometimes sharp, jeff, as in the G# between the high As in the first bar (as in the sixth setting by greatauk).
Also, on the famous “The Silver Bow” recording, I think Tom Anderson plays a C# in the scale run up near the end which, admittedly, I’ve never knowingly heard anyone else do, but it’s quite a Shetland thing to blur the lines between major and minor.

Re: Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’

“Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’ ” is Tune 14, on page 26, of “Haand Me Doon Da Fiddle” by Tom Anderson and Pam Swing, published in 1979. The book provides authentic, reliable Shetland settings of 55 tunes. It’s currently out of print but is available in PDF format via the following link:
https://ia801005.us.archive.org/18/items/haand-me-doon-da-fiddle/Haand%20me%20doon%20da%20fiddle_text.pdf

You can hear the tunes in the book here:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0D7W1tvmKrg
played by Tom Anderson and Violet Tulloch. “Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’ ” sarts at 15:13 into the video. Played a little slower than you’d normally hear a Shetland fiddler might do in a session.

Here’s a link to the Silver Bow recording DonaldK refers to:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kpiqM5ENKh8&list=OLAK5uy_kg54XikDbVN3izRAhLmwGMtWlA4FUlmgQ&index=1
“Sleep Soond Ida Mornin’ ” starts at 1:14

Re: Sleep soond ida mornin’

In part 3 (X:1) there is an unusual formula (|A gA fA g|) in the dorian mode. It reminds me of a similar formula the band Pinkfloyd used repeatedly, in order to create an unusual, charged (ominous) athmosphere in one of their pieces.
Just another illustration of how music recycles the 7 same notes -and the 49++ modal intervals**- to achieve very different effects.


** “Modal intervals”, as i call them, are not defined in absolute terms (like a semi-tone or a 9th, etc) but in relation to both a real or putative drone (= unchanging home key) and a “home mode”.
In the example above, the interval A-f# is a major 6th (= 9 semi-tones) but crucially, it is not perceived, in relation to the A drone, like c-a would be (although also a 9 semi-tone 6th). Nor is it perceived, in the context of this dorian tune, like it would if it was part (interval I-VI) of a melody in the ionian/major mode, or, indeed, as in X:9, in a mixolydian context.
(Classical and Jazz have developed concepts to describe their art: it is fair to try to understand modal music (if there is such a thing) in its own terms too).
Just by the by. :)
